name: The deleted Mars Sample Return vehicles
short_status: None reached a launch pad. From 2022 the campaign deleted its fetch rover, a second lander, two helicopters and the ascent vehicle, and ESA members asked to cancel the Earth Return Orbiter, reported on 28 March 2026.
page_title: The deleted Mars Sample Return vehicles
tagline: NASA / ESA · Multinational · Sample return · 2020 · Multipolar Mars Cancelled

facts.label: The campaign as it stood in 2021
facts.value: Three flight elements after Perseverance: a NASA Sample Retrieval Lander delivering a Sample Fetch Rover and a Mars Ascent Vehicle to the surface, ESA's Earth Return Orbiter carrying a NASA Capture, Containment and Return System to catch the sample container in Mars orbit, and an Earth Entry System to bring it down. NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center was responsible for the ascent vehicle, a two-stage vehicle with solid propulsion. The March 2021 release cited here covers the lander, the fetch rover, the ascent vehicle and the orbiter; the capture system and the Earth Entry System are described in the July 2022 release cited further down.

facts.label: Deleted: the single Sample Retrieval Lander
facts.value: At a Space Studies Board meeting on 21 March 2022 Thomas Zurbuchen said NASA and ESA had agreed to split the lander in two. Phase A analysis had shown that a single lander broke entry, descent and landing heritage and was high risk: it needed a heat shield estimated at 5.4 metres across, a larger launch fairing, unproven landing capability and electric propulsion on the cruise stage. SRL1 would carry the ascent vehicle and the sample transfer arm and be built at JPL; SRL2 would carry the fetch rover.

facts.label: Deleted: the Sample Fetch Rover and SRL2
facts.value: On 27 July 2022 NASA announced that the campaign would no longer include the Sample Fetch Rover or its associated second lander. Perseverance would become the primary means of transporting samples to the lander carrying the ascent vehicle, an assessment Jeff Gramling attributed to a recent review of the rover's reliability and life expectancy and to Curiosity's ten years of performance. NASA said it had confidence the rover would be available to deliver samples in 2030.

facts.label: How far the fetch rover got
facts.value: Not far. In October 2020, when ESA awarded Airbus Defence and Space the 491 million euro contract to build the Earth Return Orbiter, Airbus held only study contracts from ESA for the fetch rover. We found no later build contract and no record of any fetch rover being constructed. NASA's July 2022 release records that the refined concept had been presented to delegates of the 22 participating states of Europe's Terrae Novae exploration programme in May, and that at their September meeting the states would consider discontinuing its development.

facts.label: Added, then deleted: the Sample Recovery Helicopters
facts.value: Two rotorcraft based on Ingenuity, added to the lander in July 2022 as a backup path for moving tubes. Richard Cook described them as slightly heavier than Ingenuity, each with a robotic arm to grapple a sample tube and wheels on its landing legs so it could roll up to a tube after landing, fly back to the lander and roll up to that. Beyond retrieval, NASA considered using them to observe the area around the lander and photograph the ascent vehicle's launch.

facts.label: How far the helicopters got
facts.value: Into hardware testing. For three weeks in September 2023 a next-generation dual rotor system was run in JPL's 25-foot space simulator, the 8 by 26 metre chamber where Surveyor, Voyager and Cassini were tested. The carbon fibre blades were more than 10 cm longer than Ingenuity's and were spun to 3,500 rpm, 750 rpm faster than Ingenuity's blades have ever turned, reaching 0.95 Mach at the tips. Teddy Tzanetos, Ingenuity's project manager, also managed the Mars Sample Recovery Helicopters. Deputy test conductor Tyler Del Sesto said the blades were ready to fly.

facts.label: When the helicopters disappeared
facts.value: NASA's architecture announcement of 7 January 2025 describes a landed platform with a smaller Mars Ascent Vehicle, a radioisotope power system in place of solar panels, a 30-tube orbiting sample container and a redesigned sample loading system. It does not mention helicopters at all. We found no NASA release specifically announcing their cancellation. This entry states what the record shows and does not infer a date.

facts.label: The Mars Ascent Vehicle: propulsion
facts.value: On 4 March 2021 NASA awarded the Mars Ascent Propulsion System contract to Northrop Grumman Systems Corporation of Elkton, Maryland, a cost-plus fixed-fee contract with a potential mission services value of 60.2 million dollars and a maximum potential value of 84.5 million, with a 14-month base period and two option periods. Northrop Grumman was to develop and qualify two different solid rocket motors, with multiple deliveries of each.

facts.label: The Mars Ascent Vehicle: integration
facts.value: On 7 February 2022 NASA awarded the Mars Ascent Vehicle Integrated System contract to Lockheed Martin Space of Littleton, Colorado, cost-plus-fixed-fee with a potential value of 194 million dollars, for multiple test units and a flight unit plus ground support equipment. The performance period was to begin no later than 25 February 2022 and run six years. Had it flown it would have been the first rocket launched from the surface of another planet. It was replaced in the January 2025 redesign by a smaller version and then cancelled with the programme.

facts.label: The Earth Return Orbiter
facts.value: ESA's largest contribution. Airbus Defence and Space received a 491 million euro contract in October 2020 to develop and deliver the Earth Return Orbiter; Airbus in turn awarded Thales Alenia Space a 130 million euro subcontract that same month for the Orbit Insertion Module, the propulsive stage that would have put the spacecraft into orbit around Mars and then separated from it, saving mass for the journey home.

facts.label: How far the orbiter got
facts.value: Furthest of anything in the campaign. The Earth Return Orbiter passed its Platform Critical Design Review in July 2024, confirming the performance, quality and reliability of its systems and clearing Airbus to move into integration and testing. In December 2024 Thales Alenia Space announced that the Orbit Insertion Module's proto-flight model was complete, a proto-flight model being both prototype and flight-ready unit. On 28 July 2025 the company announced that the module had passed its qualification test campaign with excellent results and had been packed and shipped from Turin to Airbus in Stevenage a few days earlier.

facts.label: The Capture, Containment and Return System
facts.value: NASA's payload aboard Europe's orbiter, which would have caught the sample container in Mars orbit, sealed it and carried it home inside an Earth Entry System. It was never deleted in any redesign: NASA's July 2022 release describes the Earth Return Orbiter and its NASA-provided Capture, Containment and Return System as remaining vital elements of the programme architecture, and the January 2025 architecture still relied on it. It died with the campaign rather than ahead of it.

facts.label: The plan to save the orbiter
facts.value: At ESA's ministerial council in Bremen in November 2025 the agency proposed repurposing the Earth Return Orbiter as a dedicated European exploration mission with scientific and communications relay dimensions. The proposed mission, ZefERO, would have launched in 2032 to study Martian winds and conduct geological investigations while serving as a relay, and might have replaced the data relay function of ESA's LightShip tug. ESA also proposed a new application for the Sample Transfer Arm, supporting operations on the lunar surface.

facts.label: The cancellation
facts.value: Following a press conference after the 345th ESA Council meeting, reported on 28 March 2026, Director of Human and Robotic Exploration Daniel Neuenschwander said member states had asked for the cancellation of the Earth Return Orbiter mission. He was answering a question about the funding shortfall in ESA's exploration programme. ESA had begun discussions with Airbus to manage the transition and to maximise the return on investment on the reuse of some technology, citing the electric propulsion system as one element that could potentially be reused.

facts.label: What remains
facts.value: The samples. Ten sealed tubes lie on the ground at the Three Forks depot in Jezero Crater and the rest ride aboard Perseverance, which is still operating. NASA's Mars Sample Return page, last updated on 3 August 2026, opens in the past tense, calling Mars Sample Return a proposed multi-mission campaign and a plan for an ambitious, multi-mission campaign that would bring Martian samples to Earth. As of 24 August 2026 we could find no mission anywhere funded to collect the tubes.

timeline: ESA awards Airbus Defence and Space a 491 million euro contract to build the Earth Return Orbiter; Airbus subcontracts the Orbit Insertion Module to Thales Alenia Space for 130 million euros. Airbus also holds ESA study contracts, and only study contracts, for a fetch rover.

NASA awards the Mars Ascent Propulsion System contract to Northrop Grumman of Elkton, Maryland, worth up to 84.5 million dollars, to develop two solid rocket motors for the two-stage Mars Ascent Vehicle managed at Marshall Space Flight Center.

Lockheed Martin Space wins the 194 million dollar Mars Ascent Vehicle Integrated System contract for multiple test units and a flight unit, with a six-year performance period beginning no later than 25 February.

Thomas Zurbuchen tells the Space Studies Board that the single Sample Retrieval Lander is being split into two, because a single lander needing a 5.4 metre heat shield breaks entry, descent and landing heritage and is high risk. Launches slip to 2028 and the return date to 2033.

NASA and ESA delete the Sample Fetch Rover and its second lander. Perseverance becomes the primary means of delivering samples, with two Ingenuity-derived Sample Recovery Helicopters as backup. European states are to consider discontinuing fetch rover development at their September meeting.

For three weeks, next-generation helicopter rotors are tested in JPL's 25-foot space simulator, spun to 3,500 rpm and 0.95 Mach with carbon fibre blades more than 10 cm longer than Ingenuity's. The deputy test conductor says they are ready to fly.

The Earth Return Orbiter passes its Platform Critical Design Review in July 2024, clearing Airbus to integrate and test. In December Thales Alenia Space announces that the Orbit Insertion Module's proto-flight model is complete.

NASA announces two competing landing architectures, sky crane or a commercial lander, with a smaller ascent vehicle, a radioisotope power system replacing solar panels, a 30-tube orbiting sample container and a redesigned loading system. The helicopters are not mentioned.

Thales Alenia Space announces that the Orbit Insertion Module has passed its qualification test campaign and has been shipped from Turin to Airbus in Stevenage. It is the most complete piece of Mars Sample Return flight hardware we could identify.

At ESA's ministerial council in Bremen the agency proposes repurposing the orbiter as ZefERO, a European Mars mission for 2032 studying winds and geology and acting as a relay, and proposes a lunar role for the Sample Transfer Arm.

Congress declines to fund Mars Sample Return in the fiscal 2026 appropriations minibus, which the Senate passes 82 to 15 on 15 January and the President signs on 23 January 2026. On 28 March ESA reports that member states have asked for the cancellation of the Earth Return Orbiter, and that talks with Airbus have begun on reusing some of its technology, the electric propulsion system in particular.
NASA's Mars Sample Return mission page is updated. It now describes the campaign in the past tense, as a plan that would have brought Martian samples to Earth. Nothing is funded to collect the tubes.

images.caption: A four-wheeled Sample Fetch Rover development vehicle, nicknamed Codi and carrying Airbus and ESA markings on its wheel bogies, standing on bare excavated ground with spoil heaps behind it during ESA and Airbus field trials at Stevenage in the United Kingdom in mid-October 2023. Its blue robotic arm is extended down and forward toward a sample tube lying on the ground at the left, and a camera head and mast rise above the open tubular chassis. GMV records that the rover drove about 300 metres around obstacles and then detected and collected the tube with no human intervention, and that ESA continued the Airbus-led project after the fetch rover had been removed from Mars Sample Return.

ESA's 2019 infographic of the Mars Sample Return architecture, drawn as one continuous white line from Earth to Mars and back. Three rockets stand on Earth at the bottom, labelled Mars 2020 mission, Sample Retrieval Lander mission and Earth Return Orbiter mission. On the Martian surface the NASA rover leaves red sample canisters, a small blue ESA rover drives out to collect them and returns them to the lander, and a rocket carries the container up to orbit, where the orbiter captures it, sheds its modules and drops a capsule onto the Earth.

A NASA illustration released on 21 April 2022 showing the Sample Retrieval Lander on the Martian surface with the Mars Ascent Vehicle climbing away from it on a bright plume, the sample container inside the rocket's white nose cone. The lander stands on legs with a ring of petal-shaped solar arrays spread around it and four spherical gold-wrapped tanks on the deck. NASA's caption gives the rocket a height of about 3 metres and describes a robotic arm loading Perseverance's sealed tubes into the nose cone before launch.

A frame from a camera inside JPL's 25-Foot Space Simulator, burned in with the timestamp 2023-09-15 18:13:13, showing the dual rotor system for the next generation of Mars helicopters mounted on a steel test rig against the chamber's black corrugated wall, with a white baffle hung behind the blades. NASA's caption records that over three weeks the carbon fibre blades, longer and stronger than those on the Ingenuity Mars Helicopter, were spun at ever higher speeds and greater pitch angles and reached Mach 0.95 at the tips.

An artist's concept of ESA's Earth Return Orbiter above Mars, showing a compact body carrying a dish antenna and a payload stack, with two very long solar wings of many rectangular panels spread either side of it. The cratered limb of Mars fills the lower part of the frame, and a yellow disc on the limb at the left edge is one of a chain of lens flares thrown by the sun off frame to the right, and should not be mistaken for a moon. NASA's caption describes the spacecraft that would have been the largest ever to orbit Mars and the first interplanetary spacecraft to capture samples in orbit and make a return trip between Earth and Mars.

A photograph taken at Airbus in July 2025 during integration of the oxidiser tank into the Earth Return Orbiter's Orbit Insertion Module. The module's flight structure, its black and foil-wrapped central tube braced by blue handling beams, hangs from an overhead crane on a lifting frame above a foil-covered tank standing on a trolley; two technicians in cleanroom coveralls work at the interface ring, one of them in an Airbus suit and orange helmet with his back to the camera, and a placard on the handling frame reads ASSEMBLY WEIGHT 1050 KG. ESA's caption for the frame reads Oxidiser tank integration into the Orbit Insertion Module.
